intro: Grieg played a two-minute abridged version of Wedding Day at Troldhaugen, Op. 65 No. 6, his own wedding-anniversary march, in this acoustic recording made in Paris in 1903. The piece uses short chords, low D octaves and quick triplets.

sections.label: A · March in D major
sections.mNote: The march opens with low octaves and short chords.

sections.label: B · March theme continued
sections.mNote: Quick triplets in the piano melody

sections.label: C · Chords across the keyboard
sections.mNote: The march is set in octaves and full chords.

cues.title: Opening, played by Grieg
cues.text: Grieg marks the opening Tempo di Marcia un poco vivace, a march with a little life in it. Low D octaves alternate with clipped chords, and a quick triplet leads into the melody. Grieg himself plays in this recording, made in Paris on 2 May 1903.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Op. 65 No. 6, bars 1–10, Louis Oesterle edition, typeset by David Whipple for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O65/troldhaugen/troldhaugen-a4.pdf. Grieg’s Paris session of 2 May 1903, matrix 2149F: https://www.marstonrecords.com/products/legendary-piano
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition, summer 1896
cues.text: Grieg wrote the piece in the summer of 1896, recalling his silver wedding anniversary at Troldhaugen, when far more guests arrived than the couple had invited. His first title was “The well-wishers are coming”.
cues.evidence: Ernst-Günter Heinemann and Einar Steen-Nøkleberg, preface to Henle HN 1291 (2016), pp. III–IV: composition date, silver wedding and autograph title “Die Gratulanten kommen”, translated here. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: Letter to Julius Röntgen, 1903
cues.text: On 13 May 1903, eleven days after the recording session in Paris, Grieg wrote from Leipzig to Julius Röntgen: “I was glad to say farewell to France, and especially Paris.” The visit left nine short piano recordings, this piece among them.
cues.evidence: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, Leipzig, 13 May 1903, quoted in Marston’s Legendary Piano Recordings booklet; the same essay documents nine sides recorded in Paris on 2 May. https://www.marstonrecords.com/products/legendary-piano

composer.epithet: Son of a Bergen merchant; used Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party in concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. In his essay Min første Succes he recalled the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, but he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
